This sucks. But, as an old fart, let me give you some perspective, if I may:

You learned a valuable lesson today. Your employer will never be loyal to you. (Especially at larger companies.) They may "rah rah rah" about "team" and such but that's all BS.

As such, you don't need to be loyal to them. Your only loyalties should be yourself, your family, and your maker.

With this mindset:

  • Don't get caught up in "respect." It's empty and shallow. Do your job, do it well. If you look for or demand respect, you will come across as weak and not deserving of respect. The people who earn respect are the ones who quietly kick ass every day.
  • Work an honest day; work hard, but keep a perspective that you are just a cog and this is just a job.
  • Be nice; don't be political. It isn't worth it.
  • HR isn't your friend.
  • Be friendly but make sure you have close friends outside the job. Do well, be nice and don't worry about what others think.
  • Know that this is a job. They will come/go. You will survive and be stronger for it.
  • ALWAYS better yourself. Never assume that you have "arrived" and you can stop learning and stop improving. The only day you get to stop improving yourself is when you retire.
  • Once a year, make a new resume. Even if the job is going great. Look at this like a milestone. What was improved / what was accomplished?
  • Work towards financial independence. The more you save, the less you are dependent on the system. If you are always paycheck to paycheck then you are a modern day slave. You can't afford to say "no." The power to say "no" is absolutely amazing.

Good luck.

I agree with @mostlyfriendly here, and would add - you're clearly "proactive" so ignore this note if already know - don't wait or expect bosses to come to you when new to a company. Proactively schedule a 30-minute meeting with your boss for weekly or every 2 weeks catch-ups. Share your top 3 accomplisments, barriers and ask if there is anything you need to improve or if they believe you're meeting expectations. If you know there may be an issue with a colleague, ask them how they would handle it - no tattle telling, gossip or finger pointing. Plain old diplomacy with openess to learn from the experienced. If they reject meeting candence invite, then make a practice of weekly email to them instead. This helps you keep track, for end of year reviews, but also great to use for resume updates. Lastly, helps keep record if they come to you about an issue you asked for help on weeks prior. You won't know where you stand, if you don't ask.

If you can put politics aside for a minute - this is the reason that unions are good for employees, and why they've been demonized mostly by ultra big businesses.

Companies aren't your friends. Good work may not be rewarded and is certainly not a key to success by itself. Life is not logical and it's not fair. Unions help keep incompetents around, but they also keep the 'good guys' from getting screwed as well. Something some people tend to forget is that the incompetents aren't always on the bottom. The guy above your, or above him, or above them - they might be the least competent of all. Nepotism and good timing, more often than not, will beat merit. And the pursuit of money can even turn otherwise decent people into idiots. With a union you would have had things in your contract requiring just cause for termination, and the burden of proof would be on the employer. Hearsay being insufficient proof. And in case of wrongful termination you would have been able to have the resources to challenge it.
